note.title: Non-communicable diseases, lifestyle factors and cancer
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Non-communicable diseases come from inherited factors and lifestyle, often several together
Obesity: energy used lower than energy intake; it leads to cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes
Tar: bronchitis (narrowed bronchi and bronchioles), emphysema (damaged alveoli, less surface area), lung cancer
Nicotine: addictive, affects the heart rate. Carbon monoxide: combines with red blood cells, less oxygen carried
Alcohol: binge drinking damages the liver; in pregnancy, foetal alcohol syndrome
Cancer: uncontrolled cell division. Benign: encapsulated, does not spread. Malignant: can spread
Lower the risk: HPV vaccine (cervical), not smoking (lung), avoiding UV (skin)

notOnThisSpec: Body mass index and its calculation
Named carcinogens other than tar, and the stages of cancer treatment (chemotherapy, radiotherapy)
Metastasis as a term: CCEA says a malignant tumour is capable of spreading
Any claim that light drinking protects health: it is contested, and not on the specification

mustBeAbleTo: Recall that non-communicable diseases are caused by inherited and lifestyle factors acting together
Explain obesity as energy used being lower than energy intake, and name the diseases it leads to
Name tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide, and give the effects of each
Give the effects of alcohol misuse: liver disease, and foetal alcohol syndrome in pregnancy; read the time over a limit from a blood-alcohol graph
Define cancer as uncontrolled cell division, tell benign from malignant tumours, and read differences between cancer cells and normal cells from a diagram
Give a lifestyle choice that lowers the risk of cervical, lung and skin cancer
Use data: units against a guideline, percentages of a total, and differences read from a diagram
sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes, calculator allowed. This topic comes as short recall (the chemicals in tobacco smoke, the type of tumour, the radiation behind skin cancer), as data questions on alcohol units against a guideline or on cancer statistics, and as six-mark banded questions: the harmful chemicals in tobacco smoke (Summer 2025) and the differences between tumour cells and normal cells in a diagram (Summer 2024).
traps: Giving tar's effects to nicotine, or nicotine's to tar: every effect must sit with its own chemical (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q8, Higher Q4)
Writing 'cell division' or 'mitosis' for cancer without 'uncontrolled' or 'abnormal' (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q9, Higher Q4)
Writing 'the sun' or 'sunlight' where the mark needs UV (Summer 2024 B2 Foundation Q9, Higher Q4)
Not using the diagram: the differences between tumour cells and normal cells must be read from it, and a tumour whose cells spread into blood vessels is malignant (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q4)
Working out the percentage of a number when the number is already the percentage of a total (Summer 2025 B2 Foundation Q3, the same slip in reverse)

workedExamples.stem:
The guideline is no more than 14 units of alcohol a week. A pint of beer is 2 units; a measure of gin is 1 unit. The table shows what three people drank over one weekend, and nothing from Monday to Thursday.
Which person had the most unhealthy drinking habits? Give two reasons. [3]

steps.decision: Turn every drink into units first: pints are worth 2, measures 1. The numbers of drinks alone mislead.

options: Because a pint of beer holds more alcohol than a measure of gin
Because the guideline is written in drinks
Because people drink more pints than measures
whyMenu.explain: A pint of beer is 2 units and a measure is 1, so four pints is more alcohol than four measures. Units put every drink on the same scale.

steps.working: Person C: 16 units, more than the guideline of 14.
steps.decision: Compare each total with the weekly guideline. Only one person goes over it.

steps.working: All of it on two nights, 8 units each on Friday and Saturday: binge drinking.
steps.decision: The second reason is how quickly it was drunk. A lot in a short time is binge drinking, which damages the liver.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Person C: 16 units, more than the weekly guideline of 14, and drunk in large amounts on single nights, which is binge drinking.

twin.stem: A fourth person, D, drank 2 pints of beer on Friday and 3 measures of gin on Saturday, and nothing else that week. Calculate the number of units person D drank.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from earlier topics. Where in the lungs does gas exchange happen?
items.skill: Recall the site of gas exchange

options.feedback: In the alveoli: tiny air sacs with a huge surface area. Tar damages exactly these.
The trachea carries air down to the lungs. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.
The bronchi carry air into each lung. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.
The diaphragm is a muscle that moves air in and out. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

items.skill: Recall the role of red blood cells

options.feedback: Red blood cells, using haemoglobin. Carbon monoxide gets in the way of this.
White blood cells defend the body. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells.
Platelets help blood clot. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells.
Plasma is the liquid part of the blood. Oxygen is carried by red blood cells.

items.stem: What is mitosis used for in the body?

options.text: growth and the repair of damaged tissue
options.feedback: Growth and repair. Cancer is this same division, out of control.
Sex cells are made by meiosis. Mitosis is for growth and repair.
That is the job of white blood cells. Mitosis is for growth and repair.
Digestion uses enzymes. Mitosis is for growth and repair.

options.feedback: Tar damages the airways and lungs; the addictive chemical is nicotine.

Carbon monoxide: it combines with red blood cells, so the blood carries less oxygen.
